text: Debates over how to address structural inequality often founder on a definitional impasse: is inequity best understood as the aggregate of individual prejudices, or as something systemic, woven into institutions so thoroughly that no single actor bears full culpability? Scholars of intersectionality insist on the latter, arguing that disparate outcomes across race, gender, and class cannot be explained by any one axis of disadvantage in isolation, since marginalization compounds where these categories intersect. This framing has practical stakes: policies aimed merely at symbolic inclusion risk devolving into tokenism, a gesture that leaves entrenched hierarchies and institutionalized precarity fundamentally undisturbed. Reparative measures—targeted redistribution, for instance, rather than formally equitable but substantively hollow equal treatment—are correspondingly harder to justify politically, since they require majorities to accept a measure of collective, if diffuse, complicity in outcomes they did not personally cause. Critics on the right counter that such remedies risk entrenching group identity as the primary unit of justice, displacing older ideals of individual merit; defenders respond that formally colorblind policy, applied to a deeply stratified starting point, merely launders hegemonic advantage rather than mitigating it. Whether subaltern communities can be meaningfully included without unsettling these hegemonic structures, or whether current arrangements merely disenfranchise them further, remains genuinely contested.

They require accepting a measure of collective complicity in outcomes not personally caused

They eliminate the need for redress

That they are insufficiently equitable
That they increase tokenism

By arguing that formally colorblind policy merely launders existing hegemonic advantage instead of addressing it
By agreeing that individual merit should be prioritized
By rejecting the concept of stratification altogether
